news.title: Google unveils Gemini 4 Carbon, starting with cyber defenders only
news.summary: Google's new frontier model tops the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and scores 88.2% on the SEC-bench Pro vulnerability benchmark. Because of its hacking ability, access starts with a small group of trusted defenders before a wider release.

news.title: Mistral releases open weights for its trillion-parameter Large 4
news.summary: After a moderated preview earlier this month, Mistral published the weights of Large 4, a 1-trillion-parameter multimodal model that companies can run on their own servers. It is pitched at software development and defensive cybersecurity.

news.title: Alphabet's cloud revenue doubles, but shares slide on spending and a SpaceX loss
news.summary: Alphabet posted $127.6 billion in third-quarter revenue, with Google Cloud up 103% to $30.7 billion on AI demand. Profit fell after an unrealized loss on its SpaceX stake, and heavy data-center spending pushed the stock down sharply after hours.

news.title: Canada to take an equity stake in Cohere for up to C$1.6 billion
news.summary: Ottawa will invest up to C$1.6 billion (about US$1.1 billion) in the Toronto AI company. In return, Cohere must keep its headquarters in Canada and spend at least C$1.7 billion on domestic computing by 2030.

news.title: OpenAI rewrites its Model Spec around five core values
news.summary: The rulebook for how OpenAI's models behave is now organized around faithfulness to human intent, harm minimization, honesty, human agency and care. OpenAI says the change gives models better guidance when no specific rule covers a situation.

news.title: OpenAI expands monitoring to catch misbehaving internal AI agents
news.summary: OpenAI says its monitoring for unauthorized agent behavior now covers more of its internal operations. Replaying a past security incident, it says the system would have raised an alert about 30 minutes after the problem began.

news.title: Reddit says Google's AI Mode sends it little traffic
news.summary: Reddit's CEO said Google search referrals fell by more than a million visits a week on average in October as AI answers replace links. Reddit also plans to push more of its site behind logins to curb scraping.

news.title: Anthropic adds 20 organizations to its AI for Science program
news.summary: New partners get Claude credits and research collaboration, including work with the Allen Institute on large scientific datasets. A research preview also lets AI agents operate lab instruments.

news.title: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings agrees to buy ADT in $15.3 billion deal
news.summary: Josh Kushner's AI roll-up vehicle will take the home-security company private at $10 a share in cash, a 45.6% premium. Thrive plans to use AI to remake ADT's operations; the deal is expected to close in early 2027.

news.title: Amazon's Andy Jassy says outside AI shopping agents fall short
news.summary: Jassy argued third-party shopping agents are still less convenient than shopping on Amazon directly. The remarks follow Amazon's September move to block Meta's Muse assistant from its store.

news.title: Meta quietly launches Style Sketch, an AI wardrobe app
news.summary: The app suggests outfits from clothes people already own, can import wardrobe photos from Instagram, and offers virtual try-ons. It is live only in Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand for now.

news.title: Swing-state voters want more AI safeguards ahead of the midterms, poll finds
news.summary: Polling in competitive U.S. states shows broad support for AI safety rules. Respondents backed reasonable regulation even if it might cost the U.S. some technological edge.

papers.title: PlanWAM: Planning-Shaped Future Representations for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: A self-driving model learns to imagine only the parts of the next few seconds that help it pick a safe path, beating prior systems on the NAVSIM benchmark and a closed-loop simulator.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
PlanWAM is a self-driving system that learns to imagine the next few seconds of the road, keeping only the parts of that future that actually help it choose a safe path.

## Background you need
An end-to-end driving model takes raw camera images and directly outputs the path the car should follow. A world model is a part of the system that predicts what the scene will look like in the near future. A latent is a compact internal summary, a list of numbers the model uses instead of full pictures. NAVSIM is a popular test that scores proposed paths on safety, progress and comfort using real recorded drives.

## The problem
Many driving models add a world model, hoping foresight improves decisions. But they usually train it to redraw the future scene, or to match features from generic image models. That goal is set by image quality, not by driving needs. A model can predict every leaf on a tree yet miss a pedestrian about to step out.

## The idea
The authors flip the question: instead of asking how to predict the future, they ask which parts of the future matter for planning. It is like a chess coach who, knowing how a game ended, points out the few moves that mattered, so a student learns to spot them earlier. PlanWAM trains a "coach" that sees the real future, and a "student" that must guess it from the past alone.

## How it works
1. **Compress the past.** The car sees four recent moments from four cameras. An image encoder turns each view into tokens (small packets of information), squeezed into 128 tokens that favour recent moments.
2. **Train a coach that sees the future.** During training only, a second branch looks at the real camera frames from 1 to 4 seconds ahead. Its future summary is never asked to redraw images; it is shaped only by how well the planner and scorer do with it.
3. **Train a student that guesses the future.** A separate branch, which sees only the past, learns to copy the coach's future summary. This is called distillation (one model learning to imitate another). At driving time, only the student runs.
4. **Propose and pick a path.** The past and imagined-future tokens feed a planner that drafts 64 candidate paths for the next 4 seconds. A scorer then rates each one on six checks, such as collisions, staying on the road and comfort, and keeps the best.

## Results
On NAVSIM version 1, PlanWAM scored 93.8, versus 93.1 for the strongest prior system, DrivoR, and 94.8 for a human driver. On the stricter version 2 it scored 90.9, slightly above the human reference of 90.3. On HUGSIM, a closed-loop simulator (where the car's own choices change what happens next), it ran without extra training. There it completed 53.7% of routes on average, against 45.9% for the best baseline.

A future summary trained the usual "predict features" way scored 93.5; the planning-shaped one scored 93.8. The number of complete failures on the test set fell from 314 to 237. Collision failures dropped by about 62%. The full model takes about 342 milliseconds per decision on one data-center GPU.

## Why it matters
Self-driving teams spend heavily on world models. This work suggests a cheaper target: predict only what changes the decision. The coach-student trick could also suit robots trained on logged data.

## Caveats
Gains on the main benchmark are small, often a few tenths of a point. Failures from leaving the drivable area rose slightly. Closed-loop evidence comes from one simulator only; common tests like Bench2Drive were not reported. No total model size is given. The student still trails the coach, which scores 95.0 when it can see the real future.

## Key terms
- **End-to-end driving:** one model maps camera input straight to a driving path.
- **World model:** a component that predicts how the scene will evolve.
- **Latent:** a compact numeric summary the model uses internally.
- **Distillation:** training one model to imitate another, often stronger, model.
- **Closed-loop testing:** evaluation where the car's actions affect what it sees next.

papers.title: KV Cache Quantization for Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: Diffusion language models reuse slightly stale memory between rounds, so the authors calibrate on realistic decoding paths and keep a few key entries at full precision to compress that memory to 4 or 2 bits with less accuracy loss than existing methods.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
The authors show how to shrink the memory of a new kind of language model, the diffusion language model, by storing its working memory in 4-bit or 2-bit numbers without hurting its answers much.

## Background you need
Most chatbots write one word at a time. Diffusion language models (dLLMs) work differently: they start with a reply full of blanks and fill many blanks in parallel over several rounds. Both kinds keep a KV cache, the model's short-term memory of the text it has already processed. Quantization means storing those numbers with fewer bits, like rounding prices to the nearest dollar to save space.

## The problem
The KV cache can eat much of a GPU's memory during long replies. Squeezing it to 4 or 2 bits is well studied for left-to-right models. Those tools assume the cached memory is exact, because in left-to-right models old words never change their meaning once written.

Diffusion models break that assumption. Every word looks at every other word, even blanks. A popular speed-up called Fast-dLLM reuses cached memory across rounds instead of recomputing it. But as blanks get filled, the true memory shifts, so the reused cache is already slightly stale. The authors call this cache-reuse error. Quantization then adds rounding error on top of an error that existing methods never planned for.

## The idea
Imagine tuning a grading rubric on finished essays, then using it on rough drafts. It will be off. The authors tune on realistic in-between drafts instead. Then they keep a few especially important numbers exact, like the few line items that drive a budget.

## How it works
1. **Rebuild realistic decoding paths (TRACE).** For each prompt-and-answer pair, they work out a plausible order in which the model would have filled in the answer's blanks. This gives calibration data that matches what the cache sees during real decoding.
2. **Group the keys.** Each cache entry has a key (used to decide where to pay attention) and a value (the content retrieved). Keys are split into groups of 32 tokens, each sharing one rounding scale.
3. **Protect a few keys per group (dLLM-KVQ).** Inside each group, 0, 1, 2 or 4 key tokens stay in full precision. Candidates are ranked by attention received, rounding damage, or both.
4. **Pick the rule per layer.** For every layer, they choose the rule that best preserves attention patterns and outputs on the rebuilt paths, under a cap of 4.9 average bits per key.
5. **Quantize values plainly.** Values get ordinary low-bit rounding with no special treatment.

## Results
They tested two diffusion models of 7–8 billion parameters, LLaDA and Dream, on two math and two coding benchmarks. Baselines were KIVI and KVQuant, two leading quantizers for normal models, adapted to the same caching setup.

Their method had the best average score among quantized methods in every setting tested. On LLaDA with 2-bit prefix caching, it averaged 44.38 versus 43.62 for KIVI and 41.45 for KVQuant. The full-precision, no-cache reference was 45.96. On LLaDA with 4-bit prefix caching, it scored 45.34, slightly above the unquantized cache at 45.08.

Gains are modest, often under one point, so run-to-run noise could matter. But KVQuant collapsed on one coding test at 2 bits, scoring about 17 versus 27–28 for the others, while their method stayed stable.

## Why it matters
Diffusion models are attractive because filling many words at once can be fast. Memory often limits how many users a GPU can serve. This work gives a careful recipe for compressing their memory. It also warns that tools built for normal models carry hidden assumptions that do not transfer.

## Caveats
The paper reports no speed, throughput or memory measurements. Those would need custom GPU code, which the authors did not build. Only two models, four tasks and one decoding setup were tested, each as a single run. Protected keys push the effective key size to about 4.6–4.8 bits in the 4-bit setting, so savings are smaller than the label suggests.

## Key terms
- **Diffusion language model:** a model that writes by filling in a blanked-out reply over several parallel rounds.
- **Quantization:** storing numbers with fewer bits to save memory, at some cost in accuracy.
- **Cache-reuse error:** the gap between a reused, slightly stale cache and a freshly recomputed one.

papers.title: Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing
papers.tldr: MERLIN helps multi-memory linear attention models pick the right memory by tracking both the average and the spread of each segment's keys, improving long-context recall and beating baselines that use four times more memory.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
MERLIN gives fast "linear attention" language models a smarter way to decide which part of a long document to read from, by tracking not just what each chunk of text is about on average, but how varied it is.

## Background you need
Standard transformers use attention (each new word compares itself with every earlier word), so cost grows with the square of the text length. Linear attention models, such as Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet, instead squeeze everything read so far into a fixed-size memory called a state. That keeps cost growing only in step with length. Multi-State Linear Attention (MSLA) goes one step further: it cuts the context into segments and gives each segment its own state.

## The problem
One fixed-size state is like one notebook page for a whole book: old details get overwritten. Multiple states help, but the model must then combine answers from all of them. Today's MSLA methods weigh each segment by one number: how well the current word matches the segment's average key (a key is the vector each word offers for matching). An average hides a lot. A segment with one exact match among unrelated words can look as dull as an irrelevant one. That hurts finding a single buried fact, a core long-context job.

## The idea
Imagine picking a library shelf by its "average topic" alone. A cookbook shelf hiding one chemistry book looks like pure cooking. Knowing how mixed each shelf is would flag it for a closer look. MERLIN (MomEnt Routing for multi-state LINear attention) adds that spread statistic for every segment.

## How it works
1. **Split and compress.** As in existing MSLA models, the input is split into segments, each compressed into its own memory state.
2. **Keep two key summaries.** Per segment, MERLIN also stores the first moment (the average key) and the second moment (how the keys spread around it).
3. **Score each segment two ways.** A new word (the query) uses these to get its average match with the segment and how much that match varies. High variance hints that a few words may match strongly.
4. **Blend the readouts.** Each state returns its own answer, called a readout. MERLIN weights readouts using both scores, so promising segments count more. Variance is a "second-order" statistic, hence the name.
5. **Plug in.** The routing is a general add-on that works across different linear attention backbones.

## Results
The authors built multi-state versions of two existing models: Gated DeltaNet with 1.3 billion parameters and Mamba-2 with 780 million. They compared MERLIN against existing ways of combining per-state readouts.
- On RULER needle-in-a-haystack (hiding a fact in long text and asking for it) and long-context question answering, MERLIN improved results by 8.3% on Gated DeltaNet and 7.0% on Mamba-2.
- Across a range of LongBench subtasks (a suite of long-document tasks), gains were 13.5% and 12.0%.
- MERLIN also beat baselines using four times more memory: reading memory smarter beat simply adding memory.

## Why it matters
Linear attention models handle long inputs cheaply, but their known weak spot is recall: pulling one exact detail from far back. MERLIN targets that with light extra bookkeeping instead of bigger states. If it scales, it could help long-document assistants and agents built on cheaper models.

## Caveats
- Tests stop at 1.3 billion parameters. Larger models are untested.
- The abstract does not say whether gains are absolute points or relative.
- Storing a second moment per segment costs extra memory and compute. We could not confirm the exact overhead or training budget, because the full paper text was not reachable when this was written.
- Comparisons are against other combining methods, not necessarily full attention transformers.

## Key terms
- **Linear attention:** attention with a fixed-size running memory, so cost grows linearly with length.
- **State:** that compressed running memory.
- **Key and query:** matching vectors; the query asks "what do I need?", keys say "here is what I hold".
- **First and second moments:** the average of a set of values, and how spread out they are.
- **Needle-in-a-haystack:** a test that hides one fact in long text and asks for it.

papers.title: Less is more: learning what to profile for GPU kernel optimization
papers.tldr: Instead of feeding an AI kernel optimizer the same big profiling report every time, AutoProfiler learns a decision tree that measures only the hardware statistics each kernel needs, giving better results under a tight profiling budget.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
AutoProfiler teaches an AI kernel optimizer to measure only the few hardware statistics that matter for each specific piece of GPU code, instead of dumping the same long report on every job.

## Background you need
A GPU kernel is a small program that runs one operation, such as a matrix multiply, across thousands of GPU cores at once. Large language models (LLMs) can now rewrite kernels to make them faster. To do that well, they look at profiling data: hardware counters that record things like memory traffic, cache hits and how busy the cores are. NVIDIA's Nsight Compute is the standard tool that collects these counters.

## The problem
Today's LLM kernel optimizers pick one fixed profiling recipe and use it for every kernel. Choosing what to measure sits outside the optimization loop, so nobody checks whether it actually helps.

The authors found that collecting more metrics does not reliably produce faster kernels. The most useful metrics also change from kernel to kernel. Profiling also costs time, and long metric dumps can bury the one signal the model needed.

## The idea
Treat "what to profile" as something you learn, not something you hard-code. The authors also argue on theoretical grounds that a choice tailored to each kernel can beat any single fixed recipe.

Think of a good doctor. They do not order every blood test for every patient. They run a quick check, then order only the follow-up tests this patient needs. AutoProfiler builds that kind of decision procedure for GPU kernels.

## How it works
1. **A profiling tree.** The core object is a tree of decisions. Each node measures a handful of hardware counters on the current kernel. Based on those readings, it sends the kernel down one branch or another.
2. **Path-specific evidence.** By the time a kernel reaches a leaf, the tree has gathered a small, targeted set of metrics. Different kernels take different paths, so they get different evidence.
3. **One rewrite call.** The collected metrics go to the LLM, which rewrites the kernel once. There is no back-and-forth where the model keeps asking for more measurements.
4. **Learning the tree.** During training, an LLM proposes edits to the tree. A REWRITE edit changes what an existing node does. A SPLIT edit divides a node into finer branches. Each proposed edit is tested on real kernels and kept only if the measured speedups improve. The released code trains on a corpus of 999 programs.
5. **Fixed budget at use time.** Once trained, the tree is deterministic. Routing depends only on counter readings, and total profiling stays within a set budget.

## Results
The paper evaluates on KernelBench, a public benchmark of PyTorch operations that models must turn into faster GPU code. According to the abstract, AutoProfiler beats fixed profiling setups when the profiling budget is limited. The public code compares three strategies: no profiling, a fixed Nsight Compute recipe, and the learned tree. We could not access the full paper text for this digest, so exact speedup figures are not reported here.

## Why it matters
Most work on AI kernel writers focuses on the model or the search loop. This paper points at a quieter lever: the quality of the evidence the model sees. Better evidence at lower profiling cost could make automated kernel tuning cheaper and more reliable.

## Caveats
The tree must be trained first, which takes many real GPU runs and LLM calls. A tree learned on one GPU may not transfer to a different chip with different bottlenecks. The headline gains are stated for limited profiling budgets, so the advantage may shrink when profiling is cheap.

## Key terms
- **GPU kernel**: a small program that runs one operation in parallel across many GPU cores.
- **Profiling**: measuring how code actually behaves on hardware while it runs.
- **Hardware counter**: a built-in tally the chip keeps, such as bytes read from memory.
- **Nsight Compute**: NVIDIA's tool for collecting detailed kernel counters.
- **KernelBench**: a benchmark that checks whether AI can write correct, fast GPU kernels.
- **Profiling budget**: a cap on how much measuring is allowed per kernel.

papers.title: ASAP: Aligning Simulation and Real-World Physics for Learning Agile Humanoid Whole-Body Skills
papers.tldr: ASAP lets a humanoid robot learn athletic moves in simulation, then uses a little real-robot data to learn how reality differs and retrain the skills so they transfer faithfully.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
ASAP teaches a humanoid robot athletic moves in simulation, then uses a short session on the real robot to learn how reality differs from the simulator, and retrains the robot's skills in a corrected simulator.

## Background you need
Robots usually learn agile skills in a physics simulator, because practising on real hardware is slow, costly and risky. The trouble is the "sim-to-real gap": motors, masses and friction never behave exactly as the simulator assumes. A policy (the learned controller that turns what the robot senses into motor commands) that looks perfect in simulation can stumble on the real machine. Motion tracking means making the robot copy a reference movement, such as a recorded human jump, joint by joint.

## The problem
Two standard fixes exist, and both have weak spots. System identification measures physical settings, like a link's mass or a motor's stiffness, and plugs them into the simulator. But it only fixes the settings you thought to measure, and it often needs torque sensors that many robots lack. Domain randomization trains under many random versions of physics, so the policy copes with anything. The authors argue this makes robots play it safe, which kills agility. For a humanoid doing a 180-degree mid-air spin or a long jump, "safe but sluggish" is not good enough.

## The idea
Think of a tennis player who practised on a slow indoor court, then plays one set on grass. Instead of guessing the grass physics in advance, they notice how their shots land differently and adjust. ASAP does this for robots. It learns a small "correction" model from real-world trials, and that model nudges the simulator so it behaves more like the real robot.

## How it works
1. **Collect human moves.** The team films people doing expressive athletic motions, like famous sports celebrations and jump shots, and rebuilds them as 3D body poses. A physics-based checker throws out clips that are physically impossible, and the rest are mapped onto the body of a Unitree G1 humanoid.
2. **Pre-train in simulation.** A policy learns, through reinforcement learning (trial and error guided by a score), to track each motion. During training, the critic (a helper network that judges how well things are going) sees extra information like exact body position. The policy itself sees only what the real robot can sense, so it needs no external tracking system later. The allowed tracking error shrinks over training, from 1.5 metres to 0.3 metres, so the robot first learns to stay upright.
3. **Run it on the real robot.** The pre-trained policy is deployed, and motion capture plus onboard sensors record what really happens, alongside the commands sent.
4. **Learn the correction.** A "delta action model" is trained in simulation. Starting from each recorded real state, it learns small adjustments to the commands so the simulated robot ends up where the real one did. For example, if the simulator overrates motor strength, the model learns to weaken leg commands.
5. **Fine-tune and deploy.** The correction model is frozen inside the simulator, and the policy is fine-tuned there. The final policy then runs on the real robot without the correction model.

## Results
The authors test three transfers: from one simulator (IsaacGym) to two others (IsaacSim and Genesis), and from IsaacGym to the real G1. They use 43 motions graded easy, medium and hard, including a 1.5 metre forward jump and a 1.3 metre side jump. A trial fails if the robot's body drifts more than 0.5 metres from the reference at any moment. They compare against system identification, domain randomization and a method that learns corrections to the simulator's physics directly. The paper reports that ASAP reduces tracking error against all of these baselines, in both simulator-to-simulator and real-robot tests. In practice, that means the robot copies fast, whole-body moves more faithfully than with the usual fixes. We could not access the paper's full results tables, so exact error figures are not given here.

## Why it matters
Humanoid companies need robots that move with real agility, not just walk carefully. ASAP offers a recipe that needs only a modest amount of real-robot data and no torque sensors. The same "learn a correction from reality" idea could help other robots, from legged machines to arms, cross the sim-to-real gap faster.

## Caveats
This is an older paper (early 2025), chosen for its influence rather than recency. The real-world tests used a G1 with fixed wrists, on motions picked because they showed obvious sim-to-real gaps. The correction model is trained from the pre-trained policy's own runs, so a very different policy may need fresh real-world data. Collecting that data still requires a motion-capture setup.

## Key terms
- **Sim-to-real gap:** the mismatch between how a simulator and the real robot behave.
- **Policy:** the learned controller that maps what the robot senses to motor commands.
- **Domain randomization:** training under many random physics settings so the policy tolerates variety.
- **System identification:** measuring physical parameters to make a simulator more accurate.
- **Delta action model:** a small learned model that adjusts commands so the simulator mimics reality.

papers.title: Perception or Reasoning? Diagnosing and Tackling Reinforcement Learning Bottlenecks in VLMs
papers.tldr: A diagnostic shows whether a vision-language model's errors come from seeing or thinking, and a new RL add-on that copies the best answer's visual attention lifts small Qwen3-VL models by about 2.5 to 3 points.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
The authors build a test that tells whether a vision-language model fails because it *sees* badly or *thinks* badly, then add a training trick that teaches it where to look.

## Background you need
A vision-language model (VLM) reads images and text together and answers questions about them. Reinforcement learning (RL) here means letting the model try several answers and nudging it toward the rewarded ones. It has made text-only models much better at math. "Attention" is how the model decides which image patches to focus on while answering.

## The problem
RL's gains on image tasks are patchy. A wrong answer about a chart could come from misreading it, or from reading it fine and reasoning poorly. Those failures need different fixes. People usually guess the cause from what a benchmark is "supposed" to test, but two models can fail the same benchmark for different reasons.

## The idea
Think of a student who flunks a geometry exam. First, give them a clear written description of each diagram. If they now pass, their eyesight was the issue. Then let a top student solve it from the weak student's own notes. If that works, the reasoning was the issue. The paper calls this diagnosis PARA (Perception and Reasoning Attribution).

## How it works
1. **Find the failures.** For each model and benchmark, the authors collect the questions the model gets wrong, using 200 examples per benchmark.
2. **Test perception.** A stronger "oracle" model (Claude Opus 4.8 or GPT-5.6-Luna) describes the image without seeing the question. If the weak model now answers correctly, that error counts as "perceptual headroom": room to improve by seeing better.
3. **Test reasoning.** The weak model describes the image, and the oracle answers from that description. If the oracle succeeds, the error counts as "reasoning headroom."
4. **Fix perception with GRAD.** During RL, the model writes 8 answers per question. GRAD (Group-Relative Attention Distillation) pulls the image attention of the worse answers toward the best-scoring one. Only the final layer is supervised, and no extra teacher or labels are needed.

## Results
PARA was run on 4 models (Qwen3-VL 2B and 4B, Llama-4-Scout-17B, Gemma-3-27B) and 17 benchmarks. Its proxy holds up: answering from the model's own description loses only 0.1 to 3.4 points versus seeing the image. Bottlenecks are model-specific. On MME, Gemma-3-27B shows far more perceptual headroom (0.79) than Qwen3-VL-4B (0.38).

Standard RL helps less where errors are mostly perceptual, and more where reasoning is the gap. Existing tricks that reweight rewards or tokens did not change that.

GRAD was trained on about 47,000 image questions. Averaged over 7 benchmarks, Qwen3-VL-2B rose from 46.5 with plain RL to 49.4 with GRAD; the 4B model rose from 57.0 to 59.5. GRAD also beat three recent perception-focused RL methods, and stacking it on other RL methods added 0.7 to 2.1 points. Using a random answer as the guide instead of the best one dropped the 2B score to 45.5.

## Why it matters
Teams fine-tuning VLMs can use PARA to see which failure they face before spending GPU time. If a model mostly misreads images, more reasoning-focused RL will not help much. GRAD is cheap: no extra model runs, and no change at use time. Benchmark designers also get a way to check what their test measures, model by model.

## Caveats
PARA relies on two frontier oracles, which can be wrong too, and samples only 200 questions per benchmark. The RL trends are broad patterns, not per-task predictions. GRAD was tested only on two small Qwen models, from a single run, with no reported compute cost. Supervising more than the last layer made results worse.

## Key terms
- **Vision-language model (VLM):** an AI that takes images plus text and answers in text.
- **Reinforcement learning (RL):** training by trying answers and rewarding the good ones.
- **Headroom:** the share of current mistakes that a specific fix could recover.
- **Attention:** the model's internal focus over parts of its input, such as image patches.
- **Oracle model:** a stronger model used as a trusted reference during diagnosis.
- **Distillation:** teaching one model (or answer) to imitate another's behavior.
